Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.

Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.
Proposition 2
Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
Proposition 3
Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm) would make the tax rates voters approved in 2012 for residents earning more than $371,000 annually permanent, rather than letting them expire in 2031.
Proposition 4
Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm) would repeal the ban on state and local governments using public money to help fund election campaigns. However, public funding for the campaigns could not come from money set aside for education, transportation, or public safety.
Proposition 5
Current law allows voters to elect replacement candidates at the same time as a recall election. Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm) would let voters fill recall vacancies through a special election or appointment.
Proposition 37
Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Proposition 37 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm) would create a new homebuying assistance program and authorize $25 billion in bonds to help eligible Californians buy newly built homes with fixed-rate mortgages covering up to 17% of the purchase price. The bonds would be repaid through mortgage payments, not state tax dollars.
Proposition 38
Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of the funds would go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the other half to research grants.
Proposition 43
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would raise the vote threshold for citizen-driven local special-tax initiatives from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Proposition 44
Proposition 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm) would require Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on health care services.
Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. The official certified results of the election will be posted by Friday, Dec. 11, at sos.ca.gov/elections. (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections)

Daniella Segura, USA TODAY NETWORK
Updated Fri, October 30, 2026 at 6:45 PM UTC

California ballot measures election night results, live updates
Voting is underway in California, where voters will decide on a slate of ballot measures.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. However, it may remain unclear whether Tuesday night will bring California's ballot-measure results. California's vote-counting process (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/nation/california/2026/06/03/why-california-takes-so-long-to-finalize-primary-election-results/90388044007/) often continues for weeks after Election Day as election officials process and tally millions of ballots.
As voters weigh 14 statewide ballot measures, two proposals have drawn particular attention: one that would impose a one-time tax on California billionaires and another that would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Here's what to know about California's statewide ballot measures.
Proposition 40: the 'billionaire tax' measure
Proposition 40 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply to people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts would generally be exempt, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Taxpayers could opt to pay the tax, due in 2027, over five years, but would have to pay more.
Ninety percent of the revenue would go to health care programs, while the remaining 10% would go to education and food assistance programs.
Two countermeasures to the proposed wealth tax, Propositions 41 and 42, have also qualified for the November ballot. The initiatives are intended to limit the effects of Proposition 40 if voters approve it. Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/) would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/) would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Early polling shows voters are split on the measure. A Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/19/the-billionaire-tax-isnt-breaking-through-01125880) released Monday, Oct. 19, found that 46% of likely voters favor the measure, while 43% oppose it. A separate Independent VoterProject survey (https://www.desertsun.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/05/becerra-leads-hilton-but-governor-race-may-be-tightening-poll-finds/92102112007/) released Oct. 5 also found voters split over the measure, with 40% in favor and 38% opposed.
However, recent polling suggests support for Proposition 40 has weakened in the campaign's final weeks.
According to a Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released Oct. 28, Proposition 40 is opposed by 52% of likely voters and supported by 46%. A poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) Studies, released the following day, found a similar result: 50% of likely voters intend to vote against the measure, while 42% are in favor.
Proposition 39: the Voter ID initiative
California is one of 14 states (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) that do not require voters to present identification to cast a ballot.
Advertisement
Advertisement
According to the state's voter information guide, if passed by voters, Proposition 39 would (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf):
Require voters casting a mail-in ballot to provide a government-issued ID number.
Invalidate mail ballots should the ID number on the ballot envelope not match the ID number used when registering.
Require voters casting a ballot in person to show a government-issued ID.
Require election officials to report each year how many voters' citizenship statuses have been verified in each county.
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown the measure failing.
A UC Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/1vp9q3f9) released Oct. 29 found the Voter ID initiative trailing by a wide 20-percentage-point margin, with 57% of voters opposed and 37% in favor. A Public Policy Institute of California Poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) released a day earlier shows Proposition 39 with fewer than half of likely voters in support: 41% in favor and 58% opposed. The poll's findings are similar to those from the PPIC poll released a month earlier, which found 43% of voters in support of the initiative and 55% opposed.
Wealth tax, voter ID election night results
On Election Night, check back here to see how the statewide initiatives are faring. First results are expected to come in shortly after 8 p.m. with continued updates through Tuesday night.
Proposition 40 (and its two countermeasures)
Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm) would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires' wealth. The funds would largely go toward health care.

Advertisement
Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm) would nullify certain state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if their revenues are exempt from California's voter-approved spending cap. It would also require audits before and after implementing new special tax-funded programs.
Proposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) would prohibit new state taxes on personal property and ban retroactive state taxes based on past actions. If passed, it would also invalidate taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that conflict with these rules.
Proposition 39
Proposition 39 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm) would require voters to present additional identification to cast a ballot. If passed, the measure would require in-person voters to present government-issued ID and would invalidate mail-in ballots without the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID written on the envelope.
California voters weigh in on 10 other measures
Here's how the 10 other propositions on the ballot are playing out on election night.
Proposition 1
If passed, Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) would let the state borrow $11.25 billion to fund housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preserving existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance.

Proposition 2 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm) proposes doubling California's Rainy Day Fund, first approved by voters in 2014. The funds would support education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.

Proposition 45
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to speed up environmental review for certain housing, transportation, water, and health projects by setting deadlines for reviews and for resolving lawsuits that challenge project approvals.
When do polls close?
Polls close (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/help-strengthen-our-democracy/poll-worker-training-standards/section-three) at 8 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
When will California election results be certified?
Thursday, Dec. 3, is the last day for county election officials to certify election results (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/upcoming-elections/general-election-november-3-2026/key-dates-deadlines), which must be sent to the California Secretary of State by Dec. 4. assistantMessageEvent.content:
The election is still ongoing. Polls close on November 3, 2026, and results are not yet available.

No official results have been released yet. I am pulling PPIC crosstab data for Q32 on Prop 45 to analyze voting patterns by party.

The PPIC crosstab data for Prop 45 is being decoded. The header row lists twelve demographic columns, but the extracted numbers appear in reverse order. I am mapping the vote counts to each demographic group.

The extracted numbers are concatenated unweighted counts. A cleaner snippet shows 1076 likely voters, with yes votes at 41% and no votes at 46%. The PDF layout appears to reverse the column order during text extraction.

A second PPIC crosstab snippet reveals additional demographic breakdowns for Prop 45. The data includes age groups, race, gender, and household composition. Yes votes are 42% overall, with higher support among Republicans and Latinos.

The publication page reports a 46% yes and 50% no split among likely voters. Republicans lead with yes, while Democrats and independents lead with no. Regional support varies sharply: the Los Angeles and Bay Area regions oppose the proposition, whereas the Inland Empire and San Diego regions support it.

A September PPIC poll showed 51% of Republicans voted yes and 47% voted no. The latest poll shows 41% of Republicans remain opposed. Likely voter composition is roughly 46% Democrat, 27% Republican, and 25% independent. The October registered voter breakdown is 45% Democrat and 25% Republican.

A weighted calculation by party and region yields roughly 45.7% yes and 48.4% no, closely matching the poll topline. The undecided share is 4%, and historically undecided voters tend to break against complex propositions.

Mark DiCamillo, a leading California pollster, warns that undecided voters typically vote no and that support below 50% is a red flag. CalMatters analysis shows ballot initiative support drops roughly 6.6 to 7 points per month as the election nears. Prop 45 already lost seven points in net support from September to October.

The No side is favored to win. If the monthly decline continues, the No lead will widen. Even if support stabilizes, Yes remains below 50%. The Yes campaign has more money, but the No side has over $30 million and can sustain its messaging. The No argument against data centers aligns with Democratic voter identity. Polling shows strong opposition to AI data centers.

The No campaign has successfully linked Prop 45 to data centers, a potent late argument. Editorial endorsements are mixed and largely non-decisive. The Democratic Party official position and the official voter guide carry more weight with California voters.

The official voter guide frames the No argument as gutting environmental law and prioritizing corporate profits over public health. The Yes side only emphasizes affordability and red tape. In a Democratic electorate, that emotional framing favors No. Status quo bias also pushes undecided voters toward No.

Prop 45 spans 41 pages, so voter confusion favors No. On Point’s November 2 forecast gives No a 52.3% chance and projects a 50.2-49.8 split. It blends a structural prior of 55% yes with polls that allocate undecideds two-to-one to No, yielding a 49.8% yes projection. This is the only quantitative probabilistic forecast found, and it slightly favors No.

Yes could still win. Cost of living and housing are the top voter concerns, so the Yes message about affordability aligns with the most important issue. The campaign also has more money and newspaper endorsements. A Probolsky poll shows a thin Yes lead, but it is opaque and unreliable because of its large undecided share.

The underlying policy idea still has broad support, with 67 to 70 percent of likely voters viewing housing affordability as a big problem. The measure itself lost ground because of opposition framing, so a successful Yes reframe in the final week could reverse the trend. On Point’s model now gives Yes a 47.8 percent chance, making the race effectively a coin flip. The PPIC margin of error is plus or minus 3.8 points, so the 46-50 split is not statistically significant and the true result could favor either side.

The extracted numbers are concatenated unweighted counts. A cleaner snippet shows 1076 likely voters, with yes votes at 41% and no votes at 46%. The PDF layout appears to reverse the column order during text extraction.

A second PPIC crosstab snippet reveals additional demographic breakdowns for Prop 45. The data includes age groups, race, gender, and household composition. Yes votes are 42% overall, with higher support among Republicans and Latinos.

The publication page reports a 46% yes and 50% no split among likely voters. Republicans lead with yes, while Democrats and independents lead with no. Regional support varies sharply: the Los Angeles and Bay Area regions oppose the proposition, whereas the Inland Empire and San Diego regions support it.

A September PPIC poll showed 51% of Republicans voted yes and 47% voted no. The latest poll shows 41% of Republicans remain opposed. Likely voter composition is roughly 46% Democrat, 27% Republican, and 25% independent. The October registered voter breakdown is 45% Democrat and 25% Republican.

A weighted calculation by party and region yields roughly 45.7% yes and 48.4% no, closely matching the poll topline. The undecided share is 4%, and historically undecided voters tend to break against complex propositions.

It blends a structural prior of 55% yes with polls that allocate undecideds two-to-one to No, yielding a 49.8% yes projection. This is the only quantitative probabilistic forecast found, and it slightly favors No.

The campaign also has more money and newspaper endorsements. A Probolsky poll shows a thin Yes lead, but it is opaque and unreliable because of its large undecided share.

The underlying policy idea still has broad support, with 67 to 70 percent of likely voters viewing housing affordability as a big problem. The measure itself lost ground because of opposition framing, so a successful Yes reframe in the final week could reverse the trend. On Point’s model now gives Yes a 47.8 percent chance, making the race effectively a coin flip. PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

### Proposal
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”
Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures.
The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits.
The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.

Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

October 27, 2026 / in News, Insights & Research (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/category/news-insight-and-research/) / by Probolsky Research (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/author/probolsky-research/)
Probolsky Research regularly conducts election and public policy polling for public interest. We have released these results for California Proposition 45 on the November ballot for public interest . The company has no client in the race nor any affiliation with the respective campaigns.
“There is a clear gender divide on Prop. 45. Men support the measure 51% to 36%. Women oppose it 42% to 36%,” explained Dr. Adam Probolsky, president of Probolsky Research. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up.”

I will fetch the Probolsky screenshot and examine the PPIC crosstabs more carefully.

I will also review historical patterns for California measures polling near 46-50 percent. I am checking for UC Berkeley IGS and Emerson polls. The Probolsky image URL is ready, though web_fetch may not extract text from it. The PPIC PDF will provide regional splits and electorate demographics.

Academic literature shows undecided voters typically break heavily against complex initiatives. Prop 45 is a 41-page rewrite of CEQA, and its official title offers no clear benefit.

The voter guide frames the measure negatively, describing it as reducing what courts can consider during legal challenges. PPIC data shows 54 percent of Democrats vote no, while Republicans are largely yes and independents split evenly. That Democratic bloc is a major factor against the measure.

Republican support is weaker than expected. Only about 24 percent of the electorate is Republican, and even that bloc is split. The Sacramento Bee reported that 41 percent of Republicans remain opposed in the latest poll. The larger Democratic electorate still leans No.

The Democratic Party slate mail officially recommends against Prop 45. The Republican Party slate supports it, but the GOP is internally divided: six county parties oppose it, and Steve Hilton has walked back his support.

Polling shows a classic erosion pattern. Support dropped from 73 percent in July to 49-46 percent in September, then to 46-50 percent in October. This suggests opposition messaging is taking hold once voters see the full ballot language.

Measures polling below 50 percent in late stages usually lose, because a simple majority requires 50 percent plus one vote. California consultants generally consider 55 percent or higher as the safe threshold before election day. At 46 percent yes with only ten days left and a downward trend, the measure is in a vulnerable position.

On Point Nov 2 projects a 52.3 percent probability of No and a 49.8 percent share for Yes.

The forecast model blends a structural prior favoring Yes with poll data, yet the final projection still gives No a slight edge. Earlier fundraising advantages for Yes were largely erased by October 29, when opposition spending caught up to roughly $36 million versus $39 million raised.

Probolsky Research shows a gender split: men favor Yes 51-36, while women favor No 42-36. With roughly half the electorate being women, that gap likely pushes the overall vote toward No.

Late spending by environmental PACs and Wendy Schmidt’s over $10 million campaign is targeting undecided voters. The No message on environmental protection and corporate giveaways appears to be resonating well in California.

Probolsky’s gender breakdown yields roughly 43 percent yes and 39 percent no among decided voters. The undecided share is about 18 percent. If undecideds break evenly, Yes wins narrowly. If they favor No by two to one, No wins.

Probolsky’s high undecided rate is suspicious compared to PPIC’s 4 percent. The pollster often lacks transparency on methodology and sample size, so PPIC carries more weight. PPIC uses a probability-based KnowledgePanel and is the gold standard for nonpartisan California polling.

In terms of regions, Los Angeles and the Bay Area oppose the measure in PPIC data. Inland Empire and San Diego support it.

Los Angeles County is projected at 49.7 percent yes, and San Francisco at 54.6 percent yes. The broader Bay Area is mixed.

The No coalition includes environmental groups, labor unions, the Democratic Party, and the League of Women Voters. That combination is potent in California.

The opposition’s backing by building trades is especially damaging. Those unions typically support faster construction, so their stance against the measure undermines the jobs argument.

The Yes coalition includes business groups, utilities, and some housing organizations. Yet the measure is framed as a corporate giveaway, which hurts it in California. An oil company contributed one million dollars to the campaign. Data center concerns are a potent 2026 issue.

Governor Newsom has been a leading CEQA reformer and signed major exemptions in 2025. His refusal to support Prop 45 signals that even reform advocates consider the measure too extreme.

Attorney General Kamala Harris has also refused to endorse the measure. Her absence removes another high-profile Democratic validator, which hurts Yes among median voters who might otherwise favor faster housing construction.

Historical analogues suggest a weak track record for environmental rollback measures in California. Prop 23 in 2010, which suspended AB 32, failed. Developer-friendly measures often pass locally but struggle statewide when environmental groups oppose them.

We are now heading into the fall 2026 midterm election, almost two years into the second Trump administration.
The switch to Republican has continued at a slower pace, but it has reversed among the youngest voters and the newly registered.
Before the 2024 election, young (18–34 years old) and especially middle-aged (35–54 years old) Californians were switching from registering as either Democratic or No Party Preference—also known as independent—to registering as Republican in fairly large numbers (a net of about 120,000 total becoming Republican, or about 1.8%).
This year, middle-aged Californians are still switching away from the Democrats at about the same pace, toward a mix of Republican, independent, and other party registrations.
At the same time, the youngest age groups have seen a sharp reversal.
Those under 25 have switched mostly from independent to Democratic (a net of about 30,000 becoming Democratic, or about 1.5%), while those 25 to 34 have made few changes at all.

Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) .
